The chapter answers with a harder question: what actually matters? Not what flatters you. Not what sounds impressive. Not what creates more noise around your name.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The chapter addresses a success problem that looks productive on the surface but is disorienting underneath: too many things begin to seem important. Once recognition, options, and rewards multiply, a person can become surrounded by signals that all ask for commitment at once. The chapter interrupts that pressure by returning to a stricter question about importance.

This matters because ego likes substitutes that feel close enough to value to escape notice. Praise can impersonate importance. Visibility can impersonate relevance. Urgency can impersonate necessity. Success intensifies the risk because there are now more flattering opportunities through which the self can organize life around appearance rather than substance.

For that reason the chapter is not asking what feels strongest in the moment. It is not asking for sentimental purpose language. It is asking what actually matters enough to govern choice when ego is offering easier criteria. Value clarity is the mechanism here. Without it, the person lets success create momentum without direction.

That is how priority drift works. The person's time, energy, and judgment get pulled toward what reflects well on the self, what sounds urgent, or what increases visibility. The outside picture can still look admirable because activity is increasing. But the inner ranking is deteriorating. A person may become more committed while becoming less aligned.

The chapter answers this by restoring an importance filter. The reader has to sort commitments by what truly deserves weight, not by what flatters the current story. This is a success discipline because abundance makes confusion easier. Where aspiration lacked options, success can drown judgment in them.

The bridge forward is exact. Once importance weakens, the self becomes easier to arm defensively. Entitlement, control, and paranoia grow more easily when value clarity is gone, because ego no longer has a stable ranking strong enough to resist its distortions.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The chapter warns that success can obscure what matters by multiplying rewards, options, and visible demands. When more opportunities arrive, the person can start treating every flattering signal as if it deserves equal seriousness.

Ego drives that confusion by offering substitutes for value. Recognition becomes a stand-in for importance. Prestige becomes a stand-in for commitment. Motion becomes a stand-in for meaning. The chapter treats those substitutions as unstable because they can create an impressive pattern of life that is still misranked at its core.

So the chapter asks a stricter question: what is actually important? This is not about momentary preference or dramatic self-expression. It is about identifying what deserves enduring weight once success starts surrounding the person with ego rewards.

Without that clarity, priority drift follows. The person says yes for the wrong reasons, defends the wrong projects, and gradually allocates success toward what reflects well on identity rather than what serves something durable. The danger is not laziness. The danger is misdirected commitment that still looks admirable from the outside.

The answer is an importance filter strong enough to sort substance from image. Value clarity keeps judgment stable when success tries to make everything glow at once. Without that filter, the next deformations become easier because ego no longer has to defeat a clear ranking before it can become defensive.

That is why the chapter leads directly into entitlement, control, and paranoia. Value confusion does not remain neutral. It leaves the self easier to harden, possessive, and suspicious because the inner order that should resist those reactions has already been compromised.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The chapter goes after a polished success trap: too many things start looking like they matter, and ego loves the crowd.

Once the wins arrive, everything glows a little. More invitations. More praise. More chances to look serious, central, needed. Ego takes that flood and starts ranking by what flatters you most.

That is the con. Visibility is not value. Prestige is not importance. A packed schedule is not proof that your priorities are clean. Success can make the wrong things look urgent enough to outrank what actually matters.

So the chapter forces a harder standard. What deserves weight when the flattering options multiply? Not what feels loud. Not what looks expensive. Not what makes your name travel faster. What matters?

If you cannot answer that, drift starts wearing a suit. You become busy, visible, and misaligned at the same time. The work expands while the center weakens.

That is why this chapter comes before the defensive one. Lose the ranking first and ego will arm itself next. Entitlement, control, and paranoia thrive when nothing inside you is ranked clearly enough to push back.
